results.evidence: No statute numbers, § symbols, or penal code references appear; only general 'Sixth Amendment' constitutional language is used
Only organizations cited (NACDL, Bureau of Justice Statistics, ABA, National Legal Aid and Defender Association); no individual attorneys or legal scholars named

Body claim 'sentences three to six times longer than defendants who accepted a plea' has no inline source in that sentence or the preceding one ('The numbers are stark.'); also 'public defenders carry 200-500+ cases' (FAQ) and 'Public defenders carry 300-500+ cases' (TLDR) appear without named sources
All procedural claims are jurisdiction-qualified ('In every state', 'in most states', 'under their jurisdiction's rules', 'virtually any stage'); no bare universal deadlines stated
The post cites '*Strickland v. Washington*' as the source of the ineffective-assistance-of-counsel standard — this is a specific case citation, not Brady-as-terminology
Collateral impacts mentioned ('lose income, relationships, and stability', 'Employment uncertainty') are phrased generally with no universal licensing/voting/firearm/immigration claims

results.reason: Frontmatter has no question_count field to mismatch; body contains approximately 7 distinct attorney-directed question prompts plus a consolidated list, consistent with the post's structure.
Major factual claims are sourced inline (NACDL Trial Penalty report, Bureau of Justice Statistics, ABA/NLADA caseload standards, Strickland v. Washington); fewer than 2 claims lack attribution.
Action items use plain, direct language ('Ask this question today. Write the number down.') with no undefined jargon in instructions.
None of the banned cliches (at the end of the day, tip of the iceberg, slippery slope, double-edged sword, game changer, wake-up call) appear in the post.
Post uses second person consistently; brief third-person references to 'defendants' never run more than 1-2 sentences before returning to 'you/your'.
Sentences are predominantly active voice; passive constructions appear occasionally but well under the 30% threshold.
Key terms (trial penalty, Brady material, discovery, continuance, bar complaint) are defined or contextualized on first use; Strickland is explained as the ineffective-assistance standard.
Clear logical flow: intro framing -> 7 numbered structural realities (each problem -> context -> question -> action) -> consolidated question list -> CTA.
Post offers multiple actionable next steps: 7 specific attorney questions, free Case Progress Score link, and Case Decoder checkout link.
Action statements are direct imperatives ('Ask this', 'Write the number down', 'Bookmark it'); hedging words appear mainly in information/analysis statements where allowed.
No paragraph exceeds 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs are short (1-4 sentences) and stay under 100 words.
The seven numbered sections are roughly comparable in length; no single section approaches 50% of total word count.

Every threat (trial penalty years, caseload neglect, lost time to continuances, missing discovery, adverse judges, bad plea offers, attorney failure) is followed within 1-2 sentences by a specific question to ask or action to take.
Opens with a strong scenario hook ('no instruction manual'), middle builds with documented evidence (NACDL, BJS, Strickland), closes by empowering with a consolidated question list and concrete CTAs.

results.evidence: Post frames actions as questions to ask the attorney (e.g., 'Question to ask your attorney') rather than directives to follow without attorney guidance.
Each of the 7 sections ends with a specific 'Question to ask your attorney' proximate to the decision-action content.
Post explicitly states 'that depends on your specific facts' and avoids evaluating the reader's specific case strength or likely outcome.

Post states 'Defense attorneys can file motions to compel more complete disclosure' and asks 'Have you filed a Brady demand?' — recommending specific procedural steps/motions rather than just explaining them.
Post does not discuss immigration consequences, deportation, visa status, DACA, or green cards, so the immigration-specific redirect requirement does not apply.

Claims like 'three to six times longer' sentences and ABA/NLADA caseload standards are attributed generally to NACDL/BJS but specific collateral claims (e.g., Strickland examples of sleeping/intoxicated attorneys) lack direct statute/regulation/official citations with URLs.
Post references general categories like 'public defender offices' and 'defense attorneys' without naming specific firms or companies as recommendations.
Post avoids 'we recommend/advise/suggest' phrasing; the only first-person plural use is 'We provide research, analysis, and questions' in the disclaimer.

Opening vignettes like 'The prosecutor slides a piece of paper across the table. Two years probation' and 'You're sitting in a holding area...eleven minutes before their next client' are narrative scenarios not labeled as hypothetical or example.
Disclaimer states 'We provide research, analysis, and questions to help you work more effectively with your attorney' framing as empowerment to ask questions, not self-representation.
Post uses qualifiers like 'typically,' 'in some jurisdictions,' 'often,' and 'in most states' throughout when discussing legal rules.

Statements like 'Defense attorneys with a reputation for going to trial...extract better plea deals' and 'Attorneys who hear this question tend to communicate more consistently' imply specific outcomes without jurisdictional qualifier.
Trial penalty attributed to NACDL 2018 report, ineffective assistance standard attributed to Strickland v. Washington, caseload standards attributed to ABA and NLADA.
TLDR states public defenders carry '300-500+ cases' and FAQ states '200-500+' — a minor numerical range variance but not a contradictory legal claim; no contradictory statements about law appear.
Case Decoder framed as 'a clear analysis of your specific case...which questions apply' and disclaimer explicitly states 'We are not attorneys and do not provide legal representation.'

Opening names the fear (no instruction manual, attorney may not have time) but H2s mix action and topical — #1 'The Trial Penalty Is Real' and #7 'Bar Complaints Are Real' are topical/declarative rather than action-oriented.
Legal terms defined inline (trial penalty, Brady material, Strickland v. Washington contextualized), paragraphs stay at 1-4 sentences, action sections read conversationally.

No immediate-action block before the first H2 — the intro goes straight from framing into section 1; first concrete action ('Ask this question today. Write the number down') is buried at the end of section 1.
Each section leads with a default recommendation (ask this specific question, write the number down, set a 5-day calendar reminder) rather than presenting unranked options.
Bulleted lists stay at 3-4 items (bar complaint rights list has 4, discovery questions has 2, final question roundup is grouped by topic headers not unranked).
system-decoder-post — seven structural realities of the system paired with accountability questions.
Every scary stat (3-6x trial penalty, 97% pleas, 300-500 caseloads, Strickland low bar) is followed within 1-2 sentences by a paired question or concrete action.
No blame language — the system is framed as the source of the problem, defendant is never told 'you should have' or implied to have caused the situation.

Arc is present (fear named, system explained, questions given) but final sentence before the CTA is a generic product pitch ('Want a clear analysis...Case Decoder') rather than a standalone agency statement.
No tables, only H2 headings used, key actions bolded, sections stay within 400-550 words each, no H4+.

Every H2 section has exactly one bolded standalone sentence under 27 words ('Your constitutional right to a trial comes with an unofficial price tag measured in years of freedom.', 'Discovery isn't a delivery — it's a negotiation...', etc.) — all shareable insights, not instructions.

Both FAQ answers start with the direct answer and avoid preamble, but the first answer is 5 sentences packed with institutional-feeling list recitation ('Most defendants never learn that...that...that...') rather than a natural support-group reply.
